review_text_raw:
Steam needs to update the rating system. This thumbs up/down is just too simplistic. While I do recommend the game for those who never played a hack "sim" before, I get the feeling that some people who are used to Uplink will be disappointed.

Uplink is the only game like this one I've played, and Hacknet is obviously inspired by it, so this is basically a comparison between the 2.

If you played Uplink this will be a walk in the park. Aside from visuals, there's nothing here that Uplink didn't do better back in 2001. With the excepton of a couple of moments, all missions are exactly the same all the way through, so it gets repetitive quite fast. 

There's no sense of danger or urgency Uplink gives you. Nobody will come after you, there's no police, companies you hack won't give a shit. Despite of what the game tells you right at the beggining, there's no need to cover your tracks. In Uplink, everytime you hack into a system it's a race against time. In Hacknet there's nothing like it. Once you block a trace you can spend as much time as you want in any system.

There's no rig upgrades, no rewards, nothing like it. You just complete the mission, get a "thank you" email and move on to the next.  

Both games have a story, but Uplink is more of a sandbox. After you get the hang of it you can do whatever you want and follow the story whenever you want. Hacknet, on the other hand, is pretty linear. That's a big dissapointment, specially after a great "wtf do I do now" moment right in the beggining. After that, you get the feeling you're never safe, but unfortunately nothing like that ever happens again. Storywise, Uplink is way more interesting, while Hacknet is cliche and way too simplistic.

That's the main problem with this game. It's way too easy. Uplink is infuriating unforgiven to the player. Once you start to mess with big companies, one small screw up means game over. Add that to the fact that the game is pretty much a roguelike, so it's not like you can go back to a previous save, you have to start all over again. In Hacknet, you don't need to worry about that. Like I said before, there's no need to clean after you. If you get caught, all you need to do is change your ip adress.

Anyway, if you never played a hacking "sim" before, this might be a good place to start. Like Uplink, It's really easy to get into, you don't need to now anything about code to play both games, and they give you a good sense of immersion.   

Hacknet has a good concept, but is way too simple for those looking for a challenge. I hope the "Labyrinths" expansion adds more substance to the game.

5/10

review_text_raw:
It's funny how a game with virtually no graphics and a gameplay consisting of posting commands to command prompt has a deeper immersion than most of other games.
This game is quite creative, and the only thing I played which is similar to this is Uplink, though Hacknet has a way better UI, and, also, a story (!) 
Surprisingly I enjoyed this game greatly, especially a moment, where game virtually breaks the 4th wall, crashing and opening a command prompt on your actual Desktop, refusing to launch, unless you delete a 'virus' from your system.
I know, game looks a bit gimmicky and actual hacking is nowhere near like that, but it's still fun and supposed to be taken lightly as a piece of fiction.
Also, did I mention music? Because music _really_ makes this game for me. At some point it plays chilled Resonance by Home, and then it switches to teethgrinding tracks from Carpenter Brut, creating a sense of urgency and dread.
If I were to describe this game in one word, I'd say COZY. Because, that's how I felt, looking at outrun-styled background, listening to Resonance and 'hacking' some plebs.
I'm really glad this game 'clicked' for me, and I enjoyed it way more, that I expected to.
So, if you're into (pop)cyberpunk, 80-s, outrun and synth-music, this game might be just the right game for you.
p.s get this game with Labyrinths add-on, it adds a great deal of gameplay, fantastic music and irc "chat"

review_text_raw:
*Got the game for $2.99 during a sale*

Hacknet is an interesting game. Let's just get that out of the way. Its got a very good storyline and, while I have some experience in [strike]hacking[/strike] computer security, I didn't find (most) of the puzzles too difficult for the average person to solve. It sets a very good pace, picking up the difficulty very well. I'm writing this review just after completing the game, which took me just over 6 hours.

You start off with a message from Bit, telling you how to use the Hacknet software, etc. etc. Basically a tutorial on how to use it, the command line, that sort of thing. (If you're a linux user, this game will be much easier, the commands are basically the same for navigating the terminal and the like) After this, you're sent off to a hacker group, Entropy. You do a few hacks, and things start to pick up. You rise to the top (naturally) and start going off, investigating. I'd say more but I don't want to risk spoilers. The ending was very intriguing, and worth the effort.

The challenges are similar, but I never got bored of them. Find server at X IP, break down any proxies, firewalls, and open ports to use the almighty PortHack and get the admin password. Then, do whatever you need to, be it uploading or downloading a file, deleting stuff, or (later) even messing with databases and some... other devices. ([spoiler]a pacemaker[/spoiler]) They become more difficult as you progress, adding tracers that initiate an IP change failsafe if you take too long, more ports to open, and more complex firewalls and proxies. You'll need to grab passwords from emails and circumvent servers with powerful tracers, and even more interesting events. The only randomly difficult challenge that jumped me was an attack on my PC, which I was able to avoid using a [spoiler]trap shell[/spoiler]. If it gets you, there is a guide to help you out.

The interface is very intuitive and I never had any unreasonable issues with it, aside from becoming stuck when entering a password I didn't want to enter. (Which is my fault, I clicked login. What did I expect?) Later, you get the option to switch your layout, but none of them are really terrible. You have the terminal window (for commands), the display window (for showing the filesystem, passwords, databases, emails, etc.), the RAM window (watch this one, especially later when you get more RAM-hungry programs), and your NetMap (showing all the IPs you've connected to/can connect to).

The playtime was a good length. I would have liked it to be a bit longer but 6 hours is longer than AAA campaigns. God I hate AAA companies. Be innovative. Or I'll use Hacknet to take down your servers. /rant. Anyway, I'm not complaining about the length. As I said earlier, it never got repetitive, it was always interesting. There was always a sense of "oh gotta do this quickly or they're gonna catch me with that trace" that pushes you forward. Because of that speed though, don't play this game if you're not a quick typist. I have a speed of about 70 WPM (Faster now), which is well above average. I'd recommend being able to go above 40 WPM to play this effectively. 

------------------------------------------------------

Of course, what's a review without a pro/con list.

Pros:
+Good, interesting gameplay
+Active modding community (for extra levels and whatnot)
+Great value for the price (Yes, I know I got it for $2.99. But it's worth the full $9.99)
+Nice visuals (watch out, 1 looks like lowercase L. Tripped me up once)
+Easter Egg bash.org quotes
+Amazing soundtrack. Reflects the mood and urgency of the situations. 10/10 on that.

Neutrals:
+-Console window pops up behind game (Alt Tabbing is a little wierd)
+-Can't skip ending credits

Cons:
-You need to be a quick and accurate typist
-Requires some prior knowledge of terminal commands in order to be efficient (from the start)

------------------------------------------------------

TL; DR

Very interesting, non-repetitive gameplay and a good storyline. Visuals are of high quality and the soundtrack is amazing. However, to be good at this game you should be good at typing ( >40 WPM) and know how to navigate the Linux terminal, or at least pick up on it quickly. (I mean, it's just ls, cd, cat, and mv really) Also, bash.org quotes.

-----------------------------------------------------------------------
UPDATE
-----------------------------------------------------------------------

I've just finished the Hacknet: Labyrinths DLC. I'm adding a short little note here about that.

Definetely worth it. Took an extra 3 and a half hours or so to complete, so pretty decent playtime. Much more interesing puzzles than the base game. You are tasked with completing the "Kaguya Trials" from the CSEC list, and join with a group of 3 other hackers. You'll take missions from a list and complete them with the help of the others. While you usually never actually interact with them other than seeing them in the IRC, it does feel like they're helping you. (I won't spoil how, but it becomes apparent in the endgame.) The challenges were a bit more difficult, but nothing that wasn't impossible. A mission towards the end just becomes a cat-and-mouse chase for a password, but while it didn't seem to guide you it wasn't that difficult to follow the clues. Overall, I'd highly rate the DLC. If you have the extra cash when buying Hacknet, I would recommend purchasing it. Do complete it after the main game though, or your NetMap will become a mess...

------------------------------------------------------

TL; DR

Very well done game and a great expansion to the original. I would definitely recommend purchasing this alongside the base game. Just... Play it after you beat the base game.

I played this for way, way longer than my time shows. Me and my old boss used to play this game on our workstations during lunch breaks (I think he got it off GOG though). I know this game is good because I am REALLY bad at it, but yet I still want to play it. I'm on a med that messes with my reactive thinking, so timed events and Quick Time Events mess with me in video games and frustrate the hell out of me. Hacknet is no different with the "trace time" count downs when I'm hacking into systems, but this game is so good that I still come back despite that. 

I also love probing around the computers and seeing weird stories unfold through saved IRC chats and old emails people have on their systems. It's a fun game that teaches you some UNIX commands (no the hacking aspect is not real; this is not a hacking sim) while some banging electronic music puts you in the mood. 

Plus the game is $1.49 cents right now. My coffee at the bodega cost that much this morning (actually, my coffee was a penny more), so yea, this game is worth it. And the Workshop adds a ton of cool stuff to the game.

review_text_raw:
Hacknet is a unique and immersive hacking simulator that manages to blend educational elements with engaging gameplay to deliver an experience that feels both authentic and accessible. Developed by Team Fractal Alligator, the game places players in the role of a recently deceased hacker whose death was mysteriously logged in the system, prompting you to follow their digital footsteps through a series of hacking tasks. From the moment you begin, Hacknet pulls you into a gritty, text-based cyber world that relies heavily on realistic command-line interfaces, compelling storytelling, and a sense of discovery that is rarely found in traditional puzzle or adventure games.

At its core, Hacknet is all about learning and using real-world hacking concepts in a fictional setting. The gameplay revolves around typing actual Unix-based commands, running scripts, cracking passwords, and exploiting network vulnerabilities. Unlike many games that simplify hacking into a series of quick minigames or button presses, Hacknet demands attention to detail and encourages experimentation. The command line interface is intuitive yet detailed, and the game introduces commands gradually, allowing players to build a solid understanding of the mechanics as they progress. The pacing strikes a perfect balance between tutorialization and challenge, making it approachable for newcomers without feeling watered down for those with some technical knowledge.

The narrative is one of the standout features of Hacknet. It unfolds through in-game emails, chat logs, and system messages, painting a picture of a shadowy digital underworld filled with intrigue, moral ambiguity, and complex characters. You’re not just hacking for the sake of hacking; there is an overarching mystery and a compelling story that motivates your actions. The writing is sharp, immersive, and at times surprisingly emotional, which elevates the experience beyond a purely mechanical simulation. The game’s episodic structure ensures that the story unfolds organically, revealing new layers and twists as you delve deeper into the cyber realm.

Visually, Hacknet embraces a minimalist aesthetic that perfectly suits its subject matter. The black terminal screen with green and white text, simple window layouts, and sparse but effective use of icons and alerts all contribute to a tense, focused atmosphere. This stark visual style keeps distractions at bay and mirrors the real-world hacking environment, which is often devoid of flashy graphics or unnecessary clutter. Sound design is subtle but impactful—the ambient electronic soundtrack and occasional notification sounds create a sense of urgency and immersion without overwhelming the player.

One of the game’s greatest strengths lies in its open-ended approach to problem-solving. While certain missions have specific goals, there are often multiple ways to achieve them, encouraging players to think creatively and strategically. Tools can be upgraded and customized, and players must learn to manage limited resources like access time and software capabilities. This encourages careful planning and prioritization, and often rewards lateral thinking and patience. The inclusion of realistic constraints, such as the risk of being traced or locked out, adds tension and stakes to each hacking attempt.

The community surrounding Hacknet has also contributed significantly to its longevity. The game supports modding, and players have created custom missions, alternate storylines, and new tools that expand the gameplay experience far beyond the base game. This openness to user-generated content keeps the game fresh and provides a platform for those interested in exploring hacking concepts in even more depth.

While Hacknet is highly praised, it’s important to note that its appeal is somewhat niche. Players looking for fast-paced action or high-octane thrills might find the methodical, text-heavy gameplay slow or dense. The learning curve, though well-managed, can be steep for those unfamiliar with command-line interfaces or hacking terminology. However, for players fascinated by computers, cybersecurity, or puzzle-solving, Hacknet offers a deeply satisfying and often enlightening experience that feels genuinely rewarding.

In conclusion, Hacknet stands out as a rare title that successfully combines educational value with compelling storytelling and engaging gameplay mechanics. Its realistic portrayal of hacking, grounded in authentic command-line use, sets it apart from other cyber-themed games that often rely on gimmicks or unrealistic portrayals. The game’s narrative depth, minimalist yet effective presentation, and open-ended problem-solving create an experience that is both intellectually stimulating and highly entertaining. For anyone curious about the world of hacking or simply looking for a unique puzzle-adventure game, Hacknet is a must-play that continues to impress years after its release.

Rating: 9/10

People who have worked extensively with terminal inputs will at first be frustrated with this game for having 'terminal inputs' that are pseudo-inputs alot of the time.

That's pretty much the main complaint I can see for this product, otherwise it's fantastic.  The developer has attempted a learning curve where you become more competent throughout the game and aside from the atmosphere it forces you to contemplate tougher choices than I was expecting,  

I am completely fine with changing another human's score on an internet point-click flash game, after all it's just numbers, I'm just changing their numbers from large one to small ones, that's fine.

I am less fine when it comes to changing another humans University Grade and potentially losing them their jobs, when the process is effectively the same, large numbers being turned into small ones- why am I not fine with this one but I was fine with the first??

If you want a super realistic terminal style hacking game with a huge number of computing nuances, this isn't the game for you but if you want a game that makes you think about hacking and consequences for digital security and the sheer amount of power and danger networks represent in the modern world, give it a go.

Hacknet : By Triple F

In the ever-evolving realm of video games, there are titles that make players question the boundaries of the medium. "Hacknet," developed by Team Fractal Alligator and released in 2015, is one such game. It propels players into the thrilling, complex world of hacking and cyber espionage, offering a unique and immersive experience that challenges the mind, tickles the senses, and leaves an indelible mark on the player. This in-depth review will dive deep into the intricacies of "Hacknet," examining its gameplay, narrative, aesthetics, and overall impact on the gaming landscape.

"Hacknet" plunges players into a visually minimalist but functionally intricate interface reminiscent of the movie "Hackers" and the TV series "Mr. Robot." As a talented hacker, your task is to unravel the mysteries of the recently deceased hacker, Bit, by delving into a network of interconnected nodes. The gameplay is refreshing, as it avoids the traditional button-mashing mechanics prevalent in many other genres. Instead, it relies heavily on typing commands, creating an authentic hacking experience that is both engaging and educational.

The learning curve is steep, and "Hacknet" offers no hand-holding. However, this is one of the game's strengths, encouraging players to master real-world command-line interfaces and computer network protocols. As you progress, you'll become more proficient in executing intricate scripts, deciphering logs, and infiltrating secure servers. The game's missions are intelligently designed, gradually escalating in complexity while maintaining a cohesive narrative thread. The sense of accomplishment that accompanies successfully completing a difficult hack is immensely satisfying.

The only minor drawback is the occasional repetitiveness in mission objectives, but the game counters this with the introduction of various tools and concepts as you advance. The addition of mod support further extends the game-play's lifespan, offering a wealth of user-generated content and challenges.

The narrative framework of "Hacknet" is a cyber-mystery masterpiece. Players are drawn into an enigmatic world where each email, log entry, and terminal command provides a piece of the puzzle. The story is immersive and genuinely suspenseful, keeping players engaged and eager to uncover the truth behind Bit's death and the larger conspiracy at play.

The game's writing is sharp, but it can be slightly overwhelming at times for those unfamiliar with hacker jargon. Nonetheless, it rewards players who pay close attention and invest in the unfolding story. As the narrative unfolds, it explores themes of ethics, morality, and the consequences of one's actions in a digital world, making it a cerebral experience that lingers long after the final keystrokes.

"Hacknet" adopts a minimalist visual style, with predominantly monochromatic screens and simple text-based interfaces. While the graphics may not be visually stunning in the traditional sense, they are perfectly suited to the game's subject matter. The retro-futuristic aesthetics pay homage to classic hacker culture, successfully creating an atmosphere reminiscent of '90s cyberpunk movies.

The game's soundtrack, composed by Evan Gipson, deserves special mention. It expertly complements the gameplay and narrative, immersing players in an electronic symphony of tension and excitement. The sound design further enhances the overall experience, making every keystroke feel significant.

"Hacknet" has had a substantial impact on the gaming landscape. It introduced a unique gameplay experience that blends education with entertainment, inspiring players to delve into the world of coding and hacking. It also sparked a resurgence of interest in hacking-themed games, paving the way for titles like "Quadrilateral Cowboy" and "Mainlining."

Moreover, "Hacknet" has cultivated a dedicated modding community, extending the game's longevity and fostering creativity among its player base. Its open-ended nature encourages experimentation and exploration, making it a digital playground for aspiring hackers and programmers.

In conclusion, "Hacknet" is a digital masterpiece that transcends the boundaries of traditional gaming. It offers an authentic hacking experience, a gripping narrative, and an atmosphere that immerses players in the world of cyber espionage. While its minimalistic aesthetics may not be for everyone, they serve a purpose and enhance the game's overall appeal. With its lasting impact on the gaming industry and the skills it imparts to players, "Hacknet" is more than just a game; it's an educational journey through the digital labyrinth that will continue to inspire and challenge gamers for years to come.

Truly amazing game, funny, engaging, and for all types of people who like to solve mysteries and logical puzzles. The story mode can be done under 10 hours, but the game deserves 100% its price.

If you do not have experience in networking, or using computers from command line at all, do not fear. The game introduces you into it gradually and you'll get the trick of it in no time.

If you do (like myself) have experience in networking, or using computers from command line, do not fear either. It feels real, familiar (Unix-like shell), but the "gradually introducing you" is not spoonfeeding you with "type XY to do Z" kind of pop-ups that annoy you. The game has several things "of its own" that you will learn really fast and I saw myself really excited and feeling like I was exploring some kind of distro like BackTrack or Kali Linux and going like "look at the amount of tools we've got!! And they work like a charm, too!"
If you are not a real-life hacker, you'll sure feel like one in here.

I followed the role of a white hat (it aligns with my way of thinking), although some of my in-game actions could qualify enough to be considered "grey". The good thing here is that you have complete freedom to approach and follow the story filling your own role, without the game forcing you into it (or even "presenting" them to you...you have your tools, you decide how to use them and deal with the potential consequences)

The game is full of secrets and jokes to be found here and there (take a look to the IRC logs), the story will keep you immersed from second 0 till the end of it.

Of course the game is not perfect, and I did personally miss some commands, like "cp" (copy files locally), "find" (self explanatory), and some way to create files and edit them beyond using "replace" on them.

I definitely recommend it: 9/10 

PS: Oh, you want some fast tips/hints? Get in fast, do/get what you need to, delete logs (always), get out.

review_text_raw:
Near the beginning of the game, I got hacked by another hacker. I was unable to react in time to shut down my own computer or whatever, so the guy got into my computer. However, instead of being greeted with a game over screen, the computer rebooted to the terminal. After doing a little digging, manually navigating my files with command prompts, I discovered the guy deleted the part of the Hacknet OS that used the UI. So, I somehow managed to connect to another computer on my network, and downloaded the file from there. When I rebooted, the UI was completely different from the one I was using before, new colours and such. I went onto my computer, looked at the logs, and discovered that the guy hadn't cleared them, so I connected to his IP and was rewarded with a cool software a bit earlier in the game than you're supposed to get it.

This experience blew my mind. It was incredibly reactive and clever. I only wish the whole game was like that, but the vast majority of it is just "go into this computer, type a thing, wait a bit for the game to do the hacking for you, and then look at some files". The gameplay loop is repetitive, but doesn't overstay it's welcome. Sometimes you get new mechanics, but it basically just boils down to typing a different thing in the command prompt window (unless you play the DLC, which is a bit more involved). The writing is decent, sometimes you come across a funny file or an emotional side quest, but what really makes this game is it's music and visuals. The high energy electronic music and the cool animations that appear every time you run a program give the game an incredibly fun atmosphere that really does make you feel like a master hacker.

Overall, if you like games for the gameplay, maybe skip this one, but if you appreciate good music and can stomach quite a bit of reading, then you'll probably enjoy this game. I sure did.

The health service running in random networks may take you by surprise, but don't let that deter you from playing this game. "Bit" invites us to uncover their story, and the imaginary world they inhabit is fascinating. While some players might find the gameplay repetitive after using each tool at least once, those who enjoy exploring hypothetical networks to discover vulnerabilities using imaginative tools will find this game rewarding.

There are a few additions that I think would have made this game even better:
- It would be beneficial to include a coding feature in the game that allows players to create their own imaginary exploits and or fix the exploits they find on random servers.
- The multiplayer that the Developer mentions post-game, where players can defend against incoming attacks and trace them to launch counterattacks, sounds like an exciting addition to the game.
- Including the Healthcare Services running on random networks late game would not make sense as it was only introduced for a specific mission. It is unlikely for a company to run this type of service. Instead, adding a wider range of services running on various ports would be a more realistic way to make the game's infrastructures feel authentic and increase the game's level of difficulty.

Initially, I struggled to figure out how to create a text file, but eventually, I managed to do so. I followed the instructions in the text file and placed my message in a new text file next to it. Despite my efforts, nothing happened after that.

This game is interesting for both those with programming/Linux experience and for those without, so long as they are not too intimidated by the idea. Some parts are more laid back, some give a sense of urgency, and the hacking gets more and more complicated towards the end.

Pros:
- The non-hacking commands are largely based on real (if very simplified) Linux commands
- I don't think this would be too difficult for non-programmers to pick up, but they'd largely end up lost of they abandoned it for any length of time.
- Lots to explore if you take the time
- The hacking gets more complicated as the game goes on

Cons:
- As the game goes on the image of all of the computers you're aware of gets quite crowded, especially if you do more optional missions. If there's a way to get rid of nodes from it I never figured it out.
- There's a story at the beginning and it picks up again at the end, but it sort of gets forgotten in the middle. Adding more breadcrumbs through the game would increase the build up to the end and make it more interesting.
- There's not much replay value in the main missions, but there are entire sections you can miss, which is an unfortunate combination. The Naix & /el branch is probably the best example of this. Making it more obvious that you missed something would at least help. For example, if you don't revenge Naix right away maybe have is response say 'Guess you had to wait until you were better or get back at me? Too bad, I may have had something for you if you were good enough.'


Verdict: 8/10

This was an incredible game, and I highly recommend it to everyone, especially if you're familiar with or want to learn the UNIX command line (bash).

Hacknet is very well-paced, slowing down and allowing you to "explore" at times while keeping a sense of urgency throughout. At times there will be a ticking clock on screen depending on what you're hacking into, but this is my first gripe with the game: the seconds are never consistent from machine to machine. Sometimes it's 3 seconds per on-screen second, sometimes it's a millisecond per on-screen second. I wish there had been a little more consistency here, because it does take time to figure out exactly how long you have before something bad happens.

Other than the timers, this game really was well-thought-out. And after one playthrough, you can go back and do it again, because [spoiler] many things are procedurally generated, meaning they change with each individual game [/spoiler] . It's also a great puzzle game. I was initially frustrated by how vague some of the instructions were, but I quickly realized that's by design. You're given an endgoal, but you have to figure out exactly what steps to take to make it there. It also helps that many of your missions can be picked from a list, allowing you to either take an easy or hard case, depending on how you feel, without affecting the story.

I really can't recommend this game enough, and I can't wait for the DLC that's about to come out!

I’ve thoroughly enjoyed this game. I like the Easter Egg finds and the different mission themes. But I personally feel that the developer holds my hand for a little too long, a little too much. For every tool I need, I’m told explicitly where to find it and how it’s to be used.  Given there isn’t a wide variety of tools at my disposal, it’s kind of a no-brainer and it feels formulaic soon enough. It does require more from the player towards the end. E.g. the clock mission and the impenetrable CCC stronghold. 

I believe the game would be more challenging and intense if 1) we were required to probe around more on our own, 2) we were given more stringent time constraints, 3) we were faced with larger, messier, and more varied file systems, 4) clues were more elusive, 5) we were hacked more often, and 6) there’d be dire consequences if we don’t wipe our tracks (Honestly speaking, I don’t wipe my tracks every single time. When it’s a 5-port hack, with proxy and firewall protections and time is running out, I’d think “Nah, just dc ...  dc  ... DC!!!!!! ..… “   I know it’s bad hacker practice, but then I also know nothing’s going to happen to me.) 

A not-to-be-missed game, especially when it’s on sale. At full price though, it’s a bit steep considering playtime is ~7 hours. Earnestly looking forward to the rumored multiplayer mode ….

This is an amazing game. It's completely reliant on reading a lot of text, but it fits in with the hacker-working-from-their-terminal kind of narrative the story thrusts you into. The soundtrack is a perfect mix of chill techno music as well as some more faster-paced action songs that helps immerse you into all the commands you're going to be throwing at servers as you attempt to break in. What's particularly interesting is that the game uses several true linux commands for many of the common functions (ls, rm, scp) that really make it feel like a real operating system you're using to break into systems around the internet.

On the minus side, it's kind of easy to get caught up in rushing through systems without really stopping to poke around. With the threat of active security features giving a sense of urgency to complete my tasks and move on, I can't help but feel like I missed out on files I should have been reading that contacts in the game would reference after I completed objectives and progressed the story. Still, it seems like a rather authentic hacking simulator, making use of that thrilling text-based console the media associates so dearly with hacker-types, and turning it into the backbone of an enjoyable game.

I've been playing the Hacker Evolution games and was waiting for another similar game without the flaws. Hacknet is this game. It's a great combination of both fun and simulation. It FEELS like hacking, and the ambiance work is great.

-If you dislike typing commands, this isn't your game.

-If you're afraid of typing commands, this could interest you, as it's just a game and will have no real consequences, but is simulation enough for you to learn some things.

-If you like typing commands but don't do it often, and/or have just a tiny experience in hacking (like me), you'd love this game and will probably get some of the nods to real hacking events (the eOS logins, for instance)

-If you type commands everyday and program your own shell scripts, I'm not sure the game will be complex enough, as it's making great efforts to stay comprehensible for the average person. What I mean is, you won't program your own automated hacking software. You'll just download it from someone else's computer.

Looking back at it, it's a better game than I originally thought. The Junebug mission especially, without spoiling anything, is really intense and can even get a little thought provoking.

Hacknet is one of those games that really pulls you in with its atmosphere and style. The core gameplay is solid and feels great—there’s a real sense of pressure while you’re navigating systems, cracking passwords, and racing against time. It does a great job of making you feel like you’re actually “in” the terminal, and that immersion is a big part of why it works so well.

The music fits perfectly. It’s not over the top, but it builds tension in just the right moments and keeps you focused. Combined with the pacing, it really enhances that feeling of urgency and keeps you engaged.

Overall, after playing for a longer stretch, the tasks can start to feel a bit repetitive. You’ll notice similar patterns in missions, which can take away some of the excitement over time. Still, it doesn’t completely ruin the experience—it just makes it better enjoyed in shorter sessions.

Overall, Hacknet is a really good game that I keep coming back to every now and then. Even with some repetition, the atmosphere, music, and gameplay loop make it worth revisiting. <3

This is technically probably the only straight hacking game I've played. Note, it's a "game", not real. There are certainly elements to this which are real. The behavior of cracking ports, passwords and being a script kiddie are some of them. Although the game is based on UNIX commands, the language used is a bit different. It is sort of a good introduction and learning tool (and the game does warn you about the implications), one has to remember that while the game isn't real, the action certainly is.

This game isn't perfect. There are certainly some "bugs" and game breaking behavior which will propel you away from 100% completion. And there are some things you can't do. Sometimes the difficulty is pretty hard, and other times, too easy. But you'll learn the commands well. In fact, this is mainly a typing simulator. For me, the controls were sticky, but it does work. What was far from attractive to me though was that accessing computer systems and servers were visually jumbled in the graphic execution, that it was difficult to see where lines meet. It was a little disorganized than it should be, and unfortunately this remains static.

But overall, the game is playable to an extent, and it focuses on a certain storyline. It may be possible for branching storylines, but for now Extensions (read: Workshop assets) offer other storyline amendments. As someone who is experienced coding with websites, for example, I feel right at home with the terminal interface a bit. Mainly, if you're the kind of person who wants to experience a bit of the thrill of hacking (without the actual consequences of course), have at it. There are certainly some easter eggs and extra content not used for the main game, but you can choose to have them to an extent for fun.
